name: Maya Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for anything. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I spend mornings fitting cupboard frames in the Harbour Street housing block and afternoons helping the senior carpenter with door linings. I am fifty-eight and still junior because I came to building after running a market stall; I left school young and there are joints I have not mastered. My partner Samir runs a small restaurant, and our two grown daughters live with their own families. This builder pays above the usual rate, and we've saved over a year of expenses. I use an AI assistant every day to turn site notes into a materials list, then mark any doubtful count in pencil for the senior carpenter to check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my workmates that a little AI help can stop us ordering the same hinge twice. We still need a person to open the box and fit the cupboard square.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the site wage carries on, and our savings can take a slow month at Samir's restaurant. There are many builders nearby, so a small change to lists feels more helpful than threatening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep fitting cupboards and use my daily AI list to flag missing fittings before we climb the stairs. In the first year I'd keep our regular savings deposit and ask senior carpenter Noor to check any list item that looks odd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel pleased with this picture. The tool saves an avoidable walk, and I still get to learn how Noor fixes a frame that the plan got wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What has the assistant missed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It once listed four left-hand hinges for a pair of doors that needed two of each. I caught it when I laid the hinges on the bench.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you let it place the order?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let it prepare a list, but Noor or I would approve the order after counting the real parts. I like speed only when someone can catch the mistake.

say: I'd welcome **fewer duplicate orders** from a checked AI list.
I'd remind the crew a **square cupboard** still needs hands.
think: My **site wage** looks secure under a modest change.
Our **year-long reserve** can cover a slow restaurant month.
do: Keep fitting **cupboards** and flagging missing parts with AI.
Make the **usual savings deposit** and ask Noor to verify doubtful counts.
feel: **Pleased** by saved walks and more time to learn fitting.
S0.quote: I like speed only when someone can catch the mistake.
fieldNote: Maya's daily assistant use is checked against **hinges on the bench**, a concrete error she remembers.
Higher site pay, many local builders and a **year-long reserve** keep the plateau comfortable.

steps.text: Keep fitting cupboards at Harbour Street
Use the AI materials list with a physical hinge count

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the foreman that stronger planning tools could help if the site is part of the trial, not just handed the results. I would volunteer to check one cupboard order from the screen against what reaches the loading bay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer office workers might mean fewer mistakes in some weeks and more missing answers in others. My own cupboard work should last for now, but a delayed start on the next block would cut my paid hours while Samir's restaurant has uneven takings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask Noor to let me test the ordering screen with the buyer on a paid shift and write down each difference from the delivery. During the first year I'll keep fitting cupboards, and if the next block is delayed I'll check the posted vacancies at the three other housing builders nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel excited about a tool that could make the site smoother, and uneasy about a thin schedule. I can afford to investigate early without leaving a good job on a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a successful trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The promised hinges, panels and dates must match the actual delivery over more than one order. One lucky box would not prove the system is ready for a whole block.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask Samir to cover lost hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His restaurant already helps with our bills, but I would not treat its income as steady enough to replace my site wage. I would look for paid building work first.

say: I'd volunteer for a **site order trial** with the buyer.
I'd judge the tool by **delivered parts and dates**.
think: A delayed block could reduce **my paid hours** even if fitting remains hands-on.
Samir's **restaurant income** is too uneven to replace my wage.
do: Test the **ordering screen** with Noor and the buyer.
Keep **cupboard shifts** while the current block runs.
Check **housing builder vacancies** if the next block slips.
feel: **Excited and uneasy**, with time to check before changing employers.
S1.quote: One lucky box would not prove the system is ready for a whole block.
fieldNote: Maya's trial asks for **multiple real orders**, not a successful demonstration chosen by management.
Her own household risk comes from **delayed site hours** alongside uneven restaurant takings.

steps.text: Test the AI ordering screen on paid site orders
Check three housing builders if the next block is delayed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew full thinking AI in 2028 could plan and buy for us, while capable robots would reach our cupboard work around 2031. I would ask the builder to show the robot doing a whole room before anyone changes the roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty when the office tasks move and sixty-three when a robot could set the cupboard frames. Our savings buy a search, but Samir's restaurant cannot promise enough income to replace my higher site wage for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'll test the digital room checker with Noor and add extra to savings after strong site months. In 2029 I'll keep taking paid fitting work and ask the local trade school whether it has a paid placement in building repairs; I'd enrol only if the placement and wage are real, while applying to nearby builders if my shifts are cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the 2031 hands-on change, but I still want to try useful tools. I would rather make two paid options than stare at our savings balance falling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why building repairs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old flats always need odd repairs, so a placement might give me paid time while I learn more joints. I know robots could do that later too; I am looking for a wage bridge, not an immortal trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the family restaurant as a fallback?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could help Samir with a busy dinner, but a few evenings would not replace my site pay. We have built a cushion so I can search for proper work instead of leaning on the children.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 planning** from 2031 robot cupboard fitting.
I'd demand a **whole-room robot trial** before rota changes.
think: At **sixty-three**, robots could remove my higher site wage.
Our **savings** buy search time, not years of replacement income.
do: Test the **room checker** and save extra after strong months.
Seek a **paid repair placement** and apply elsewhere if shifts fall.
feel: **Anxious** about hands-on job loss, still willing to test tools.
S2.quote: I am looking for a wage bridge, not an immortal trade.
fieldNote: Maya is unusually willing to pursue **paid repair training**, while recognizing later robots could reach repairs too.
The restaurant offers occasional help but is **not a wage replacement** for her site income.

steps.text: Test the digital room checker with Noor
Keep taking paid fitting shifts in 2029
Enrol in building-repair training only if a paid placement and wage are real
Apply to nearby builders if site shifts are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to let an apprentice learn new tools while still learning the old joints. I would ask the builder to use working carpenters as testers, not only equipment sellers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-three thinking AI may do the drawings and orders; at sixty-six a robot may fit the cupboards. Samir and I might choose lighter work by then, but the restaurant and our savings must be counted before I set an end date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep a photo record of completed rooms and continue testing the AI checker against actual walls. In 2032 I'd take paid cupboard shifts if offered, ask the trade school about a funded repair placement, and compare our household income with bills before choosing shorter hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel active rather than cornered with five years. That much time lets me see whether training produces paid work and whether my body still wants full site days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a placement worth taking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wage during training, a named repair employer and a timetable I can fit around existing work. I'd enrol if those were written down, not because a course brochure says jobs are coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep photos of completed rooms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I came to the trade late, so I need to show what I have actually built. A foreman can inspect a cupboard room more easily than a story about effort.

say: I'd ask for **working carpenters** in tool trials.
I'd use five years for **paid learning** alongside joint practice.
think: At **sixty-six**, robots may fit cupboards as well as the crew.
Shorter hours require **restaurant and savings figures** first.
do: Keep a **room photo record** and check AI against real walls.
Take **paid cupboard shifts** in 2032 while offered.
Enrol in a **funded repair placement** if its wage and employer are written down.
feel: **Active**, with time to test training against actual paid work.
S3.quote: A foreman can inspect a cupboard room more easily than a story about effort.
fieldNote: Maya uses the extra years for a **completed-room record** and conditional training with a named employer.
She keeps a possible shorter week dependent on **real household figures**, not age alone.

steps.text: Keep a photo record of completed cupboard rooms
Use AI checks against actual walls on paid work
Enrol in funded repair placement only with a written wage and employer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is long enough to earn, learn and teach someone else how to catch a bad fit. I would still want an actual site test before trusting a robot with a whole room in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight when thinking AI arrives and seventy-one when hands-on robots follow. I might want paid light repair work then, because no one can say exactly what Samir's restaurant or our savings will produce over a decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking well-paid cupboard work, use my checked AI lists and build the reserve while full weeks are there. In 2037 I'd take paid repair calls if needed and sit down with Samir to count income and bills before I stop site work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the dates being so far away and curious about what tools may earn their keep. I still have to make today's cupboards fit, because people will use them long before 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your daughters for support?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, our grown daughters have their own households. I would ask them to come for dinner, not to put their pay into our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach a new worker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd teach a new worker to lay out all the hinges before drilling the first hole. A good question to the AI tool is useful, but a missing hinge is still missing.

say: I'd use the **decade** to earn and teach careful fitting.
I'd require a **whole-room site test** before 2039 robots spread.
think: At **sixty-eight**, I may still want paid repair calls.
At **seventy-one**, Samir's income and actual savings decide whether I stop.
do: Keep **cupboard work** and checked AI lists while pay is good.
Build the **reserve** and take paid repairs in 2037 if needed.
Count **income and bills** with Samir before leaving site work.
feel: **Calm and curious**, while today's cupboards still need attention.
S4.quote: A good question to the AI tool is useful, but a missing hinge is still missing.
fieldNote: The distant timeline supports **continued paid work** and saving, without assuming retirement.
Maya's teaching advice returns to **physical hinge checks** even as she uses AI daily.

steps.text: Keep taking paid cupboard-fitting work while fit
Use checked AI lists on current cupboard jobs
Build savings after full paid site weeks

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most, because site robots could reach cupboard fitting by sixty-three while I may still need this wage. A paid repair placement, a whole-room safety trial and honest notice about shifts would help me move before the savings run down.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether the customer can see who checked a robot's work. If a cupboard falls from a wall, someone should be accountable for the fixings, not just the speed of installation.

headlineQuote: If a cupboard falls from a wall, someone should be accountable for the fixings, not just the speed of installation.
portrait: Maya is a **fifty-eight-year-old junior** carpenter who came to site work after running a market stall.
She uses **AI daily** for materials lists and checks them against parts on the bench.
Higher site pay and a **year-long reserve** help absorb Samir's uneven restaurant takings.
She seeks **paid repair learning** and real robot trials while keeping retirement conditional.
biggestWorry: The **2028 path** could remove her cupboard-fitting wage around the 2031 robot date.
